Google Cloud Content & Editorial

Want to know the latest from Google Cloud? Find it here in one handy location. Check back regularly for our newest updates, announcements, resources, events, learning opportunities, and more.

Tip: Not sure where to find what you’re looking for on the Google Cloud blog? Start here: Google Cloud blog 101: Full list of topics, links, and resources.

Oct 26 - Oct 30

  • Simplify PostgreSQL Monitoring with the New AlloyDB Omni Web UI

    The newly released AlloyDB Omni Web UI delivers a centralized, graphical dashboard that simplifies the management of self-managed PostgreSQL workloads across hybrid, multi-cloud, and air-gapped environments. This browser-based console provides database administrators with deep, real-time insights into cluster health, hardware utilization, and active database connections. It also features built-in query diagnostics and performance tracking for AlloyDB’s columnar engine, enabling quick troubleshooting of bottlenecks without manual terminal commands. To learn more about setting up this monitoring interface, read the fullAlloyDB Omni Web UI Blog Post.
  • Leveraging "Antigravity" to architect high performance semantic model routers in Apigee

    Semantic model routing replaces rigid static paths with a lightweight helper model to dynamically classify and dispatch intent-driven LLM traffic. Join Saravanakumar Rajagopal on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 5:00 PM CET for a Community TechTalk exploring how to leverage Antigravity and skills to architect these intelligent multi-provider routing patterns natively inside Apigee. Discover how to optimize your AI infrastructure and enhance flexibility at scale.

    Register for the November 12 Community TechTalk

Oct 19 - Oct 23

  • From prompt to production: End-to-end AI workflows in Apigee

    Deploying an enterprise AI gateway does not require deep API or machine learning expertise. Using declarative workflows in Apigee, teams can spin up a fully governed LLM gateway in minutes using a few environment variables. Join Luis Cuellar on Thursday, October 29, 2026 for a Community TechTalk exploring end-to-end AI workflows. Discover how to layer essential defenses—including Model Armor for prompt protection, Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP) for sensitive data redaction, rate limiting, and response caching—before routing autonomous agent interactions through your gateway filters.

    Register for the October 29 Community TechTalk
  • Zero Standing Privileges with PAM: On-Demand Temporary Access for Humans and AI Agents

    AI agents now hand work off to other agents, risking stacked privileges and overpermissioning. Because agents plan their actions on the fly, permanent admin access means one hallucination can cascade into production. Join us on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 8:30 AM PST to see how Google CloudPrivileged Access Manager (PAM) brings Zero Standing Privileges to AI delegation, putting humans in command with cloud-native control that doesn't slow developers down.

    Register for the November 18 webinar
  • Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs

    Native streaming support is now in Public Preview for API Gateway, enabling you to run real-time and AI workloads behind your existing gateway. You can now route Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding without modifying your API spec or managing a split estate. This update also strengthens integration with the Gemini platform, allowing you to stream responses from Gemini, Claude, and OpenAI gpt-oss models seamlessly while maintaining consistent authentication, rate limiting, and observability.

    Read the blog to get started

Oct 12 - Oct 16

  • AI tokenomics in action: Enforcing tiered token budgets with Apigee

    Scaling artificial intelligence across an enterprise requires clear token governance to keep LLM spend predictable across departments. Join Tarun Abraham on Thursday, November 5, 2026 for a Community TechTalk on AI tokenomics. Discover how to use Apigee to enforce isolated, tiered token budgets and model access for each team—such as assigning Engineering a dedicated budget for Gemini Pro while covering mixed usage for Marketing—without changing application code. Attendees will also gain access to a sample codebase featuring a reusable Shared Flow.

    Register for the November 5 Community TechTalk

Sept 28 - Oct 2

  • Claude Sonnet 5.5 is now available on Google Cloud. Built for focused coding and knowledge work, it delivers stronger performance for feature development, and creating presentation-ready documents, while offering more intelligence with a lower cost per task for most work at faster speed.

    Deploy Sonnet 5.5 directly from Model Garden with Google Cloud’s enterprise security, scale, and governance built in. Try it now.

  • Mastering Storage Management with Storage Intelligence

    In our new blog, explore practical strategies to modernize storage operations using Storage Intelligence Advisor and enhanced Batch Operations. See how customers like Shipt and Palo Alto Networks are using these features to manage their estates at scale. Today, Storage Intelligence is used by 25 of the top 50 GCS customers. 2 in 3 customers have Storage Intelligence enabled for over 90% of their storage footprint.

    Explore best practices on our blog
  • Cut Gen AI costs by 70% with Apigee X dynamic routing

    Generative AI deployments face a harsh cost-performance trade-off: static model selection either wastes budget or compromises quality. Discover how to build an Intelligent AI Gateway using Apigee X to dynamically evaluate prompt complexity in real-time. This new blueprint automatically routes simple queries to lightweight models (like Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite) and complex reasoning tasks to advanced models (like Gemini 3.7 Flash), achieving over 70% cost savings without sacrificing output quality.

    Read the guide to optimize your Gen AI architecture
  • AI Agent Clinic launches new hands-on session on production agent evaluations

    A new episode of the AI Agent Clinic is now available showing organizations how to move past manual "vibe checks" to build robust, production-grade agent evaluations. In this hands-on session, Google Cloud engineer Dani Zamora and Matthew Feroz (Merge) take DocsHound, an open-source LangGraph agent, and build an end-to-end eval pipeline in under an hour. Learn how to standardize multi-turn traces across any framework using OpenTelemetry and OpenInference, pair LLM judges with deterministic checkers, and catch silent quality regressions before shipping.

    Watch here
  • Drive AI impact: Join Google's Agentic Data Cloud event on Nov 4

    Every enterprise plans to adopt agentic AI within two years, but data bottlenecks hold them back—AI accesses just 45% of enterprise data today (MIT, 2026). Google's Agentic Data Cloud provides the trustworthy foundation and real-time context AI needs.Join our product leaders November 4th to explore the latest innovations across databases, analytics, business intelligence, and storage, and get direct answers in our executive Q&A with Google Data Cloud VP & GM Andi Gutmans.

    Register today!

Sept 21 - Sept 25

  • Master MCP tool authorization and agent governance with Apigee

    While the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solves interoperability for autonomous AI agents, chained actions like CRM edits or database queries quickly expose systems to unauthorized execution. Join our technical deep dive on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 5:00 PM CEST featuring Christophe from Google Cloud. Learn how positioning Apigee between MCP clients and enterprise backends enables fine-grained authorization (FGA), complete audit trails, and policy evaluation via emerging standards like OpenID AuthZEN.

    Language and accessibility note: This session will be hosted in French, but non-French speakers can follow along seamlessly by turning on Google Meet live translated captions to read in English, Spanish, German, Portuguese, or Italian.

    Register for the October 1 Community TechTalk
  • Apigee Trace Viewer Tutorial: Capturing & Analyzing Proxy Traces

    Streamlining API proxy debugging just got easier with a new tutorial by Apigee Customer Engineer Tyler Ayers. The guide covers end-to-end instructions for capturing debug traces in both Google Cloud Apigee X (or Hybrid) and the local Apigee Emulator, extracting trace JSON data via the web UI or automated REST APIs, and analyzing execution flows, variable mutations, and latency bottlenecks using the open source Apigee Trace Viewer.

    Read the Apigee Trace Viewer guide today.
  • Automate Apigee proxy testing locally

    Catching errors early saves time and money. A new tutorial by Apigee customer engineer Tyler Ayers shows how to use the Apigee Local Emulator for automated testing. Learn to run tests locally, integrate them into CI/CD pipelines, and deploy on Google Cloud Run for shared sandboxes. This approach provides instant feedback and zero cloud costs, helping teams speed up deployment cycles.

    Read the tutorial
  • Scale your enterprise multi-agent systems with Apigee

    Deploying multi-agent architectures in production introduces critical hurdles around security, operational control, and runtime expenses. Discover how Apigee API Hub provides a central discovery surface to eliminate agent sprawl across tools, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and enterprise APIs. Learn how to turn existing backend services into secure MCP tools using Agent Gateway guardrails, while applying semantic caching and intelligent model routing to keep compounding token costs predictable.

    Join Google Cloud in Chicago in Oct.15 for The AI Evolution.Reserve your seat for Chicago
  • Automate Apigee proxy testing with the Apigee Local Emulator

    Waiting on remote deployments to validate API proxy logic slows down release cycles and increases infrastructure overhead. Join Nigel Walters on Thursday, October 8, 2026, at 5:00 PM CEST for a Community TechTalk on shift-left testing for Apigee. Discover how to use the Apigee Local Emulator and apigee-emulator-service to run sub-second assertion suites on local machines, automate CI/CD checks in GitHub Actions, and deploy ephemeral preview sandboxes on Google Cloud Run.

    Register for the October 8 Community TechTalk
  • Now in Public Preview: AI-assisted EKS-to-GKE migrations with deterministic guardrails

    Migrating complex Kubernetes estates from AWS EKS to GKE is traditionally high-friction and error-prone. Now in Public Preview, GKE Agentic Migration is an open-source agent plugin that replaces ad-hoc LLM prompting with an AI-assisted migration workflow protected by deterministic guardrails.

    Running locally in your development harness, it indexes source IaC, maps cloud-specific primitives (such as Karpenter to Custom Compute Classes), and validates configurations offline—delivering reviewable pull requests and data-migration runbooks with zero live cluster mutations.

    Learn more in theannouncement blog and try the plugin on GitHub.
  • Claude Opus 5.5 is now available on Google Cloud. Built for everyday complex tasks, it delivers stronger agentic coding, research, and analysis while handling long-running work at a lower cost per token. Google Cloud continues to provide enterprise customers with broad model choice to build, deploy, and scale their AI agents securely.

    Try ithere.
  • Import Delta Lake tables with Dataflow Job Builder!

    Migrating to borderless Lakehouse just got a lot easier. You can now import Delta Lake tables stored in Cloud Storage usingDataflow Job Builder, a no-code/low-code interface for authoring Dataflow pipelines. Because Dataflow is a fully managed service, you are spared the overhead of provisioning and managing virtual machines. For step-by-step guidance, check out the documentation here.

Sept 14 - Sept 18

  • Storage Intelligence Advisor for Google Cloud Storage is now GA

    Google Cloud Storage customers can now manage cloud storage more effectively with Storage Intelligence Advisor, delivering curated metrics, automated anomaly detection, and actionable recommendations right out of the box, with zero setup required.

    Advisor baselines activity across your projects and automatically detects four key anomalies: surges in operations, unexpected rises in cross-region egress, and spikes in errors. Each finding includes deep drill-down visibility into the resources driving the change, alongside prescriptive steps to remediate issues before they impact performance or cost.

    Learn more to get started with Storage Intelligence Advisor.
  • Build private WebSockets from Apigee X to Cloud Run

    Real-time AI agents and streaming architectures often require persistent, bidirectional connections. A new implementation guide by Apigee Customer Engineer Joel Gauci demonstrates how to establish private southbound connectivity between Apigee X and Cloud Run. Using Private Service Connect (PSC) and a Regional Internal Application Load Balancer, teams can enforce API governance and security policies at the edge while keeping backend services completely isolated from the public internet.

    Explore the step-by-step guide and open-source code
  • Connecting Gemini Enterprise Agent Runtime to Apigee with Private Service Connect 

    Deploying autonomous AI agents often presents security, compliance, and cost challenges. A new reference guide details how to build an end-to-end, private architecture between Gemini Enterprise Agent Runtime and Apigee. This design helps protect internal backends and manage token quotas.

    Read the full community guide and deploy the code
  • Discover what’s new and next in Apigee

    As enterprise architectures adapt to generative AI and autonomous workflows, Apigee is expanding its proven platform capabilities to support modern AI gateway use cases alongside traditional API management. Join our session on Thursday, September 24, featuring Apigee Product Manager Geir Sjurseth. Get an inside look at recent product releases, explore architectural patterns for securing models and agents, and bring your questions for the live Q&A.

    Register for the September 24 Apigee product update
  • Managed Service for Apache Kafka supports clusters with public Internet access!

    WithManaged Kafka public clusters, you can now produce and consume messages from clients outside your VPC—including your local machine, for faster, frictionless testing. Public clusters unlock use cases like IoT devices, retail storefronts, and telco network towers. Enable public access on new or existing clusters via the Google Cloud console, gcloud CLI, or REST API. Spin up your first public cluster, or reach out to kafka-hotline@google.com with questions.
  • Stream data directly into Bigtable using Bigtable subscriptions, now in Preview!

    You can write Pub/Sub messages to a Bigtable table with zero ETL withBigtable subscriptions. No pipelines, no code, delivered by the serverless, zero-ops experience you already know with Pub/Sub. Power your AI workloads, from model telemetry to real-time context engineering, without the overhead of managing complicated ETL pipelines. Built to be dependable, with native support for dead-letter topics. Try the feature today!

Sept 7 - Sept 10

  • Why Your Voice Agent Needs Session Auditing

    Moving voice agents to production demands robust quality monitoring. This guide dives deep into the inner workings of the Agent Development Kit (ADK) responsible for audio session auditing. Learn how the ADK's
    save_live_blob
    feature intercepts, buffers, and stores raw audio chunks during active Gemini Live sessions. We explore building an automated post-processing pipeline to seamlessly stitch these fragments into cohesive, playable audio files. Discover how to leverage these vital audio audit trails to monitor real-world interactions, diagnose failures, and ensure enterprise-grade reliability. Read the full guide here.
  • AlloyDB Omni Red Hat RPM Orchestrator now Generally Available

    AlloyDB Omni Red Hat RPM orchestrator is now Generally Available. The AlloyDB Omni Red Hat RPM orchestrator offers a new way to manage PostgreSQL-compatible workloads on bare metal or VM platforms, combining the high performance of AlloyDB, access to generative AI features and Gemini models to build AI agents and applications, and full automation. The orchestrator simplifies cluster provisioning and lifecycle management by allowing you to define reference architecture specifications, customizable by adjusting instance parameters, node configurations, and networking options — discover all details in full blog post.

Aug 31 - Sept 4

  • Automate VM guest software lifecycle with VM Extension Manager, now GA

    Google Cloud VM Extension Manager is now generally available, eliminating the need for custom startup scripts to manage guest OS extensions across Compute Engine fleets. Define declarative, project-wide policies that enforce desired software states across all regions and zones. Benefit from continuous drift detection with automatic self-healing, multi-zone phased rollouts with automated rollbacks on failure, and centralized fleet health visibility integrated with Cloud Monitoring.

    ExploreVM Extension Manager documentation
  • Assess Apigee migrations without a target environment

    Planning a migration to Apigee X or Hybrid? You can now assess your legacy Apigee Edge SaaS or OPDK environment earlier in your planning cycle. Using the updated --skip-target-validation flag in the Apigee Migration Assessment Tool, teams can generate a full inventory and establish scope baselines before target infrastructure or IAM credentials are provisioned.

    Read the guide to learn more.

  • Claude Fable 5.1 is now available on Agent Platform. It brings performance improvements over Fable 5 across reasoning, full-lifecycle coding, multi-tool workflows, and knowledge work.

    Anthropic also announced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, a solution that gives customers the option to safely deploy Anthropic’s most capable models while storing their data in cloud infrastructure they control.

    We continue to offer enterprise customers options across frontier models to build, deploy, and scale securely on Google Cloud.

Aug 24 - Aug 28

  • Grok 4.6 is now available in Preview on Gemini Enterprise. xAI's most capable model, built for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work, Grok 4.6 joins Grok 4.3 and Grok 4.20 in Model Garden and becomes the flagship of the Grok family. It supports reasoning, function calling, and structured output for multi-step agentic workflows, and accepts text and image input.

    Get started today
  • Empowering autonomous agents with advanced security governance

    AI agents offer incredible productivity gains, but granting them access to read emails, query databases, and trigger APIs introduces critical new security risks. In fact, 79% of tech leaders cite security and governance as their biggest challenge to scaling AI. Traditional tools are no longer enough to handle automated threats like prompt injection and dynamic permissions. Discover how forward-thinking enterprises are using secure-by-default design, agent identity governance, and human-in-the-loop controls to deploy agents with confidence.

    Read more
  • Stateful processing is available in BigQuery continuous queries in Preview

    Stateful operations significantly expand what’s possible with BigQuery continuous queries. This feature allows users to leverage functions like JOINs, aggregations, and windowing functions directly in their streaming queries. Now you can calculate metrics over time (for example, a 30-minute average) to power your downstream applications and AI agents with much richer, real-time signals.
  • Try out our feature here and share your feedback with bq-continuous-queries-feedback@google.com!
  • Synthetic data generator tool is available for Managed Service for Kafka

    You’ve launched your first Kafka cluster. Now what? The next thing to do is to produce some data to the cluster, but that involves modifying a client application somewhere or spinning up a virtual machine. The synthetic data generator tool, now generally available, can start sending mock data to your cluster in 3 clicks, and will get data streaming into your cluster in less than two minutes. The perfect utility for those moments you just want to test your cluster and new features. Tryour quickstart today!
  • Dataflow pipeline updates are faster & more flexible

    Dataflow pipeline updates can now stop-and-replace pipelines, a major addition to the existing in-place-update feature. The new parallel pipeline option accelerates the migration between the old & new pipeline, resulting in reduced disruption to your business. You can also set a timeout on drains that prevents runaway costs for your pipeliness in the event of stuck processing. This feature is generally available. Try it here!

Aug 17 - Aug 21

  • Webinar: Agent Identity as the backbone for secure AI innovation

    An AI agent with a stolen API key looks identical to a legitimate one. As autonomous agents scale across enterprise systems, static credentials and legacy IAM policies can no longer keep up with machine-speed execution. Join Shaun Liu, Product Manager at Google Cloud, on August 27 at 1 PM ET to explore Google Cloud’s vision for unifying agent, human, and nonhuman identity into a workload-centric platform using verifiable cryptographic identities (SPIFFE, ID-JAG, OAuth).

    Register for the webinar now

Aug 10 - Aug 14

  • Diagnosing Apigee Hybrid Cassandra Read Latency for Peak Performance

    Diagnose real-time Cassandra read latency and resolve API key verification bottlenecks in Apigee Hybrid with this step-by-step troubleshooting guide. Learn how to deploy a debugging client and query performance tables to maintain sub-millisecond response times.

    Read the Apigee Hybrid Cassandra Troubleshooting Guide
  • Keep moving with agents! The All Things Agentic Hackathon is officially live.

    We're challenging builders to build next-generation agents that take on the busy work and handle the heavy lifting in the background using Gemini 3.5 and Google Cloud. Compete for your share of $190,000 in prizes, cash, and Google Cloud credits! Submissions are open from August 3, 2026, to August 31, 2026.

    Learn more and register. Sign up for GEAR to get exclusive updates and your badge. #AllThingsAgenticHackathon
  • Accelerate PostgreSQL migrations using Gemini in Database Migration Service

    Enterprise database migrations often stall during the "last mile" of translating legacy stored procedures, triggers, and custom functions from Oracle or SQL Server. Database Migration Service (DMS) now provides AI-assisted code conversion powered by Gemini in Databases. By combining deterministic compiler rules for 1:1 syntax with Gemini contextual synthesis for complex procedural blocks, DMS converts legacy code into native PostgreSQL and AlloyDB with full schema awareness and side-by-side validation.

    Read the full blog post to learn how to streamline your database code conversion.
  • Compute Flex CUDs now available for G2 and G4 GPU VMs

    Compute Flexible Committed Use Discounts (Flex CUDs) are now available for G2 (NVIDIA L4) and G4 (NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000) VMs. You can now lock in predictable savings while retaining the flexibility to adapt across VM families, migrate between regions, and combine general-purpose compute, GKE, Cloud Run, and G2 & G4 GPU VMs under a single spend commitment. Flex CUDs for G-series VMs let you lock in savings today while preserving the agility to upgrade to latest hardware without disruption!

entries.title: When the Kubernetes API went silent: A three-layer networking mystery
entries.summary: Every support engineer has a case that stays with them. The one that comes up at team lunches. The one where, even after it's resolved, you find yourself staring at a packet capture at midnight just to make sure you really understand what happened. This is that case. It started in January 2026 with a support ticket that read deceptively simply: pods are intermittently failing to reach the Kubernet
entries.content:
Akash Thakur

Sr. Technical Solutions Engineer

Every support engineer has a case that stays with them. The one that comes up at team lunches. The one where, even after it's resolved, you find yourself staring at a packet capture at midnight just to make sure you really understand what happened. This is that case.

It started in January 2026 with a support ticket that read deceptively simply: pods are intermittently failing to reach the Kubernetes API server. The error was a familiar-looking timeout. The customer had already ruled out their own operators. What none of us knew yet was that we were looking at three separate bugs — in three different layers of the stack — all conspiring to produce the same symptom at the same time.

By the time it was over, around 800 developers had been blocked from deploying to production for weeks on end, and GKE clusters across europe-west had ground to a halt. In a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself.

This is the story of how we got there.

Part one: The alarm bell that wouldn't stop

The customer ran a large multi-cluster GKE environment in Google Cloud's europe-west region. Their clusters used Private Service Connect — Google Cloud's mechanism for exposing the GKE control plane privately — and had a rich ecosystem of system-level workloads: Twistlock security scanners, External Secrets Operator for secrets management, Cilium for network policy, as well as several internal Kubernetes operators.

The first errors appeared in one of its user acceptance testing (UAT) clusters in europe-west, and a few days later in a second cluster in the same region. They looked like this:

Application logs — pods across multiple namespaces

Initially the errors were intermittent — spikes in the logs, not a hard outage. The customer suspected their own code. Their team had recently deployed a custom operator built with the kopf framework, and it was the first thing they looked at. But the logs showed the errors had started eight days before the operator was ever deployed. When they shut it down completely, the timeouts kept coming.

The issue persists even after completely scaling down the External Secrets Operator. The errors are appearing from customer workloads, and system-level pods we haven't touched.

The growing list of suspects

When a case like this arrives, the first instinct is to ask: what changed? The customer's timeline gave us several candidates, and we worked through them methodically.

  • The custom operator (kopf): Ruled out immediately — errors predated deployment by a week and continued after shutdown.

  • External Secrets Operator: Removed entirely on customer request. Timeouts continued in customer workloads that relied on Kubernetes control plane (KCP) connectivity, and cluster-internal system pods.

  • Security agents: Uninstalled. Same result. We were now watching system-level Kubernetes components fail to reach their own control plane.

  • conntrack table exhaustion: One theory was that too many half-open connections were filling the OS connection tracking table on the control plane nodes. We checked. The conntrack table was at roughly 50% capacity — of a default maximum of 1.3M entries. Not even close to exhaustion.

  • Control plane overload: We scaled up the KCP VM size. kube-apiserver latencies looked healthy. No improvement on the timeout side.

What made this case genuinely strange was the scope. We confirmed the timeouts were happening across five different clusters, affecting DaemonSets, Deployments, and system pods alike. External clients — developer laptops, GitHub Actions runners — were also hitting the same wall. This was not a broken workload. This was something wrong with the path between everything and the API server.

The timeline so far

  • Day 1: First I/O timeout errors appear (One of the UAT clusters in europe-west3. Intermittent, easy to dismiss.)

  • Day 10: Errors become persistent (Frequency increases significantly. The issue is no longer dismissible.)

  • Day 15: Case escalated — P0 bug filed (Multiple clusters confirmed affected. ~800 developers blocked. Production releases are frozen. Formal escalation begins.)

  • Day 20: All obvious suspects ruled out (Custom operator, security agents, conntrack exhaustion, control plane resizing — all cleared.)

  • Day 22: Packet captures collected (Captures taken simultaneously at the control-plane node NIC and from inside the kube-api container. The investigation enters its most critical phase.)

With the obvious suspects cleared, and the scope undeniably wide, we did what you do when the application layer has nothing left to say: We went to the packets.

Part two: Tracing the ghost in the wire

To understand what the packet captures revealed, you first need to understand the architecture that a GKE pod traverses when it makes an API call. In a Private Service Connect-based GKE cluster, the path is deceptively long for something that looks like a local connection.

The key component here is Private Service Connect. When a pod dials 1.2.3.4:443, it is not actually going directly to the control plane; that IP is a virtual endpoint. The connection is intercepted by Google's networking fabric, NAT'd through a Private Service Connect endpoint, passed through an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer, and ultimately delivered to the KCP VM, where Envoy acts as a local proxy in front of the actual kube-apiserver process.

Private Service Connect adds a proxy protocol header to each new connection, so the kube-apiserver can see the real client IP. This will turn out to be important later.

What the packets revealed

When we captured simultaneously at the KCP VM's NIC (the PIGv interface, Google's programmable virtual NIC) and from inside the kube-apiserver container, we saw something striking.

SYN packets from the pods were arriving at the KCP VM's NIC. They were getting that far. But instead of receiving a SYN-ACK in response — the expected second step of a TCP handshake — the client was getting back an out-of-place ACK. Not an RST. Not silence. An ACK that logically belonged to a different, earlier connection.

Wireshark, the network protocol analyzer, was flagging these streams with a label that initially seemed innocuous: "TCP Port numbers reused."

Wireshark — packet stream showing the failed handshake

The pattern was clear. Something was causing the KCP VM to respond to a fresh SYN with an ACK that belonged to a different connection that had ended minutes ago. The old connection had used the same source port (53426 in the example above), and the KCP VM had never fully let go of it.

"The KCP server sends FIN,ACK; client responds with FIN,ACK and then ACK. But KCP receives ACK before FIN,ACK. KCP server never ACKs the FIN,ACK — continuous retransmission of ACK. RST does not clear state."

The "Invalid ACK" spike

While one thread of the investigation was analyzing packet captures, a.k.a., pcaps, another team was digging into internal metrics for the Private Service Connect infrastructure — specifically the user space packet switch (USPS), Google's software switching layer that handles NAT and proxy protocol header injection for Private Service Connect connections.

They found something alarming in the metrics for Andromeda, Google's networking fabric. A counter called "Proxy protocol drop: invalid ACK packet" had been flat for months — and then, in February 2026, it spiked sharply upward to several drops per second across the affected europe-west regions.

That date matched a USPS version rollout. This version included a change which was a fix for a different bug but something about it had changed the behavior of how Private Service Connect handled a specific class of packet.

Challenge ACKs: The RFC 5961 mechanism

To understand the next piece of the puzzle, we need to talk about a TCP security mechanism called the challenge ACK, defined in RFC 5961.

Imagine a TCP connection has closed — gone through the FIN/ACK dance and terminated. The server-side (here, the KCP VM) may still briefly remember the connection's sequence numbers in its TCP state machine. Now imagine that shortly afterward, a new client connection arrives on the same source port and destination port (the same 5-tuple). From the kernel's perspective, this could be a stale packet from the old connection, or it could be an attacker trying to inject data into what the kernel thinks is still an open session.

RFC 5961 says: when you receive a SYN that matches an existing or recently-closed connection's remembered state, don't accept it blindly. Send a challenge ACK — an acknowledgment that carries the last known sequence number of the old connection. If the new client is legitimate, it will see this unexpected ACK, recognize the connection is stale, and send a RST to clear the state. The server then accepts the next SYN normally.

The challenge ACK flow — how it's supposed to work

This mechanism works perfectly — when the challenge ACK is allowed through. But that was exactly what the new USPS change was blocking.

The culprit: A well-intentioned fix

The change in USPS had been designed to fix a legitimate security issue in Private Service Connect's proxy protocol handling. Part of its effect was to drop packets it classified as "invalid ACKs" during the connection handshake phase — specifically, ACKs that arrived before the initial SYN-ACK had been sent, which in normal circumstances would be anomalous.

Unfortunately, challenge ACKs look exactly like this: They arrive from the server before the new handshake has completed, in response to a SYN. From the USPS's new perspective, they looked like invalid packets. They were dropped silently.

Why this broke GKE specifically: Private Service Connect uses NAT to share a single public endpoint across many client pods. This means many different pods — running on different nodes, from different namespaces — can all end up using the same source port after NAT, creating a high rate of 5-tuple collisions. The challenge ACK mechanism was being triggered far more often than it would be in a normal direct-connection scenario. The USPS fix hadn't introduced challenge ACKs — they had always been there. It had introduced the dropping of them, which broke a flow that GKE's TCP stack had silently depended on to clear stale state.

Mitigation: Rolling back the change

In February, we rolled back the USPS change, restoring the old behavior where challenge ACKs were passed through instead of dropped. The rate of "Proxy protocol drop: invalid ACK packet" dropped back toward baseline almost immediately.

By early March , 2026, the customer confirmed that all affected clusters had recovered. No more timeout errors.

But the rollback wasn't a fix. It was a band-aid. It restored the behavior the system had accidentally depended on. The deeper question — why was the KCP VM in FIN_WAIT_2 for over two minutes in the first place? — was still completely unanswered.

That question led to Part 3. And it's where things got genuinely strange.

Part three: Three bugs, one crime scene

The mitigation bought us time, but it left a question hanging in the air: Why did the KCP VM keep connections in FIN_WAIT_2 for so long? A well-behaved TCP stack processes a FIN, acknowledges it, and closes the connection. The KCP VM was failing to do this, leaving half-open connections that persisted for more than two minutes — long enough for the port to be reused by Private Service Connect's NAT layer, long enough to cause the challenge ACK scenario we'd uncovered.

To answer this, we needed to understand not just one bug, but three distinct failure modes that had intersected at the worst possible moment.

Bug #1: Packet reordering at the PIGv

The first piece was discovered through careful analysis of simultaneous captures at two points: the KCP VM's host NIC (inside the physical host running the VM) versus the PIGv — the virtual NIC as seen by the VM.

At the host NIC level, packets arrived in perfect order. But by the time they crossed through USPS and appeared at the PIGv, they had been subtly reordered.

This happens because of how Private Service Connect's miss-thread processing works. When Private Service Connect intercepts a new flow it hasn't seen before (a "miss"), it processes that packet through a slower path that adds the proxy protocol header and sets up NAT state. Subsequent packets in the same flow take a fast path. The consequence: a FIN or RST packet belonging to a flow in mid-close might arrive slightly out of order relative to the ACKs that followed it.

What the KCP VM actually received (reordered sequence)

The reordering put the client's FIN after the server had already sent its own FIN. The server entered FIN_WAIT_1, then FIN_WAIT_2 after seeing the client's ACK of the server's FIN. But then the client's own FIN arrived — and the server's kernel ignored it.

Bug #2: Envoy's half-close and the frozen timer

Why couldn't the operating system clean up on its own? There is a Linux kernel parameter called tcp_fin_timeout that governs exactly this: how long a socket in FIN_WAIT_2 waits before being forcibly closed. On the KCP VM, this was set to 60 seconds.

But tcp_fin_timeout only applies to orphaned sockets — sockets that no process is currently holding open. Envoy, the proxy that sits in front of kube-apiserver on the KCP VM, was performing a half-close: it called shutdown(SHUT_WR), which closes the write side of the connection but keeps the socket open so it can still receive data. This is perfectly valid TCP behavior and is how graceful half-duplex termination is supposed to work.

The side effect: As long as Envoy held the socket with SHUT_WR, the kernel did not consider it orphaned. tcp_fin_timeout never started. The socket sat in FIN_WAIT_2 indefinitely, waiting for a client FIN it would never be able to process correctly.

Kernel socket state — captured via netstat just before a new connection

Bug #3: The Linux kernel's silent failure

But there was still a missing piece. Even with the reordered FIN, a healthy kernel should still process a received FIN in FIN_WAIT_2 and move to TIME_WAIT. The socket should eventually close. Why wasn't it?

This led us deep into the Linux TCP state-machine implementation. When the reordered client FIN arrived at the KCP VM, the kernel's tcp_ack() function was called to process it. And here, in kernel version 6.1 (which underpinned the Container-Optimized OS (COS) running on the KCP VMs), there was a bug.

RFC 5961 added stricter validation for acceptable ACK numbers — specifically, an ACK could be considered valid even if it was slightly "old" (within a sequence number window), to handle network reordering. But in kernel 6.1, there was a code path where tcp_ack() returned zero — indicating "this packet was not fully processed" — when it encountered an ACK that was old but within the RFC 5961 acceptable window. The caller of tcp_ack() in the FIN processing path checked this return value, saw zero, and did… nothing. The FIN was received and silently discarded.

The Linux kernel commit that fixed it (upstream)

The bug had existed since kernel 6.1 and was already fixed in kernel 6.9.7 — but GKE's KCP VMs were running COS builds based on 6.1 and 6.6. The fix needed to be backported and shipped as a COS image update.

How the three bugs combined

Individually, none of these three issues would have caused an outage of this magnitude. It took all three acting together to create the failure:

  • Bug #1 alone: Packet reordering is mildly disruptive, but the kernel would normally still eventually process the FIN and clean up, just slower than ideal.

  • Bug #2 alone: Envoy's half-close is perfectly correct behavior. It only becomes a problem if the FIN is never properly processed.

  • Bug #3 alone: The kernel's failure to process old-but-acceptable ACKs would cause some connections to linger, but the impact would be limited without the port-reuse pressure from Private Service Connect NAT.

  • All three together: Reordering causes the FIN to arrive out of sequence; the kernel bug prevents it from being processed; Envoy's SHUT_WR prevents the timeout from firing; the socket stays in FIN_WAIT_2 indefinitely. Private Service Connect NAT reuses the port. challenge ACK is sent. The USPS fix drops it. Connection fails.

The resolution: A three-pronged fix

Resolving this required action at three different levels, coordinated across multiple teams over several weeks:

  • Immediate mitigation (Feb, 2026): Rollback of change in USPS. Restored the previous behavior where challenge ACKs were forwarded rather than dropped. Customer clusters recovered by early March.

  • Correctness fix: A replacement change to handle the challenge ACK scenario properly in the Private Service Connect proxy protocol layer, rather than simply restoring the old drop behavior. A PacketDrill test was added to the test suite to prevent regression.

  • Root cause fix — Linux kernel patch: Upstream patch ("net: tcp: accept old ack during closing"), authored by Eric Dumazet. Merged into Linux 6.9.7. Backported to 6.6.y and 6.1.y LTS branches. — shipping in GKE 1.33.5 and later. The bug is fully resolved at the OS level for all GKE versions running these COS images.

What made this case different

Most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete.

What finally cracked it was the discipline of simultaneous packet capture at multiple points in the path. Without captures at the host NIC, the PIGv, and inside the container at the same time, we would never have seen the reordering. Without correlating those pcaps to the USPS metric spike on February 18, we would never have found the dropped challenge ACKs. And without reproducing the issue in a lab environment, we would never have found the kernel bug that made the FIN_WAIT_2 state permanent.

The other thing that made this work was the team. Over the course of two weeks, engineers from seven or eight different specialties contributed: GKE networking, Private Service Connect infrastructure, Hostnet, Andromeda, KCP, and ultimately the kernel community. No single person could have held all of this in their head. The case notes, the shared bug tracker, the meticulously collected pcaps — they were the connective tissue that let a distributed team work as one.

In the end, the customer got back to production. The kernel got a better bug fix. And the rest of us got a very good story about why packet reordering, half-closed sockets, and a well-intentioned security patch should never be allowed in the same room at the same time.

This blog is based on real case data from an anonymized customer support engagement and internal bugs. The Linux kernel fix referenced is commit 795a7dfbc3d9, authored by Eric Dumazet. Special thanks to the engineers across GKE, Private Service Connect, Hostnet, Andromeda, COS, and the Linux networking community whose work made this resolution possible.

entries.title: ARTEX and Friends: Enter Agentic Offensive Frameworks
entries.summary: Written by: Aurora Blum, David Mainor, Rohit Nambiar, Omar ElAhdan, Matthew McWhirt, Will Silverstone, Bhavesh Dhake, Chris Busse Introduction Recent intrusions in which threat actors have been observed weaponizing agentic frameworks to execute highly-automated intrusions has put a spotlight on evolving adversarial use of LLMs. In our September 2026 report, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG)
entries.content:
Google Threat Intelligence Group
Mandiant

Written by: Aurora Blum, David Mainor, Rohit Nambiar, Omar ElAhdan, Matthew McWhirt, Will Silverstone, Bhavesh Dhake, Chris Busse

Introduction

Recent intrusions in which threat actors have been observed weaponizing agentic frameworks to execute highly-automated intrusions has put a spotlight on evolving adversarial use of LLMs. In our September 2026 report, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) noted that forward leaning adversaries were beginning to transition from basic prompting to agentic workflows and LLM-enabled automation. 

Since this publication, GTIG and Mandiant have observed multiple threat actors abusing the open-source, agentic pentesting frameworks ARTEX, Hexstrike and CAIRN in incident response engagements to conduct a broad range of actions across multiple phases of the attack life cycle. This activity has been seen across the threat landscape, as noted in a recent Wiz report. The emergence of Artex and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses.  

This represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling intrusions exponentially. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge. Security teams, developers, and system administrators will need to fundamentally rethink defense strategies to counter scalable, autonomous software. We also provide defensive strategies from Mandiant Consulting. The defensive strategies suggested—control-plane isolation, short-lived credentials, least privilege, segmentation, and behavioral detection—are long-standing security best practices.

Observations in the Wild

We are seeing tools used by adversaries evolving towards autonomous agentic attacks. One way this is occurring is through suites of tools or frameworks designed for penetration testing (“pentesting”). These tools and frameworks orchestrate various agents using open source and frontier LLMs to automate various stages of intrusions. Historically, cyber espionage and financially motivated threat actors have taken advantage of pentesting or red-teaming platforms built for security professionals to exploit systems, such as Cobalt Strike or Metasploit. Today, adversaries are pivoting toward offensive frameworks powered by LLMs. While these frameworks have existed in the wild, they are now yielding success in intrusions in the wild, representing a critical evolution that increases both the speed and scale of intrusion activity.

Since late August 2026, we have observed threat actors actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses within Mandiant incident response engagements; use of these platforms has been further corroborated by our research telemetry. In these incidents, we have observed agentic activity conducting significant parts of the attack lifecycle (e.g., lateral movement, database exploitation, exfiltration preparation). Evidence of in the wild usage of these frameworks marks a critical inflection point for defenders, as agents now autonomously explore multiple attack paths, troubleshoot errors, and achieve objectives in seconds and minutes. Coupled with continual advancements in underlying LLM capabilities, the acceleration in attack velocity and scale signals a notable shift in the threat landscape that fundamentally alters traditional intrusion dynamics.

ARTEX Framework

ARTEX is an autonomous, multi-agent LLM-driven pentesting and offensive command-and-control (C2) platform written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console. The framework was originally developed by the user Autumn-27 and released on GitHub. Although the original repository was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO. ARTEX abstracts the attack lifecycle across six specialized sub-agents. By leveraging APIs from frontier and open source models, the framework translates high-level tactical goals into actionable machine commands. GTIG has observed capabilities including automated Active Directory reconnaissance, privilege escalation, target cloud-infrastructure profiling (such as harvesting Azure storage keys), to the synthesis and deployment of custom webshells.

Since late August 2026, ARTEX has been adopted by a diverse range of threat actors across the motivational spectrum, including both financially motivated extortion groups and suspected cyber espionage operators. For example, the Wiz Research team has been tracking a campaign associated with ARTEX, which GTIG tracks as UNC7228, that overlaps with activity tracked by Microsoft as the PRC-nexus actor STORM-0940. The research has expanded Wiz’s understanding of this campaign beyond the October IT focused activity with activity now dating back to at least August 2026. Wiz identified the targeting, compromise, and data theft affecting multiple entities in the US and Europe across the enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor manufacturing and design, and telecommunications industry verticals. This actor has moved extremely quickly, typically moving from their first compromised account to deep system access in around four hours and in one case as rapidly as 15 minutes. They have also customized their tooling to take advantage of victim-specific setups and fallen back to open proxies if their initial infrastructure was blocked.

Demonstrating broader adoption of ARTEX, GTIG and Mandiant observed multiple other threat actors using ARTEX for post-compromise reconnaissance, lateral movement, and privilege escalation in incident response investigations. This includes financially motivated threat actors who used the framework to facilitate data theft extortion, and additional suspected PRC-nexus clusters. Their operations collectively impacted organizations across government, technology, chemicals and materials, and manufacturing sectors in the US, alongside public reporting of ARTEX targeting the financial sector in Asia. 

In several cases, adversaries provided ARTEX with compromised credentials for the targeted organization, and instructed the framework to execute subsequent stages of the attack lifecycle. Analysis of these intrusions reveals key differences between activity conducted by the ARTEX framework and that of a human operator:

  • Based on log files and timestamps, we identified bursts of activity that would be highly irregular for a human operator. While each of the intrusions exhibited extended pauses during operational phases, individual ARTEX execution sequences ran in compressed bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds. In at least one operation, we observed 27 events in 23 seconds of active burst time, performing rapid probing of AWS permissions across different security groups. While preparing potential exfiltration scripts, ARTEX was capable of successfully adapting to errors quoting “script too large” by trimming the script and relaunching it to successfully deploy a 17-snapshot instance in approximately 10 seconds.

  • Compared to a competent human operator, ARTEX achieved code execution in a far more forensically noisy manner, relying on rapid, iterative trial-and-error. In one instance, supplied with valid credentials, ARTEX accessed an external-facing Linux Weaver OA web server to execute SQL commands via exposed API calls. Using legitimately-exposed application-specific API calls, ARTEX was able to achieve partial command-execution to conduct further reconnaissance despite hitting technical complexities. However, this process generated 240 log events and exhibited errors potentially caused by multiple sub-agents overwriting one another while pursuing the same objective.

  • In an attempt to pivot from a database-execution context to a system-execution context, ARTEX used an application-specific SQL API, accessible to the supplied-user credential, to modify the MySQL instance to write log files with a

     .jsp
    extension to publicly accessible locations. The SQL-commands executed were likely intended to poison MySQL logs into writing web-accessible JSP webshells.

  • Using the API, ARTEX ran 

    SET GLOBAL general_log_file = '’

    general_log_file

    cl1217.jsp, f1219a.jsp, z1219.jsp
    ) for each webshell candidate, each one executing a different command. Errors when trying to run the webshell (e.g.

     .jsp
